name: Hydrogen
found: The most abundant element in the universe — it makes up most of the Sun and stars, and on Earth it is locked into water and nearly every organic molecule.
uses: Refining petroleum, making ammonia for fertiliser (the Haber process), hydrogenating fats, and as a clean fuel in fuel-cell vehicles and rockets.
daily: Two hydrogen atoms sit in every drop of water you drink, and hydrogen fuel cells now power some buses and cars with only water as exhaust.

name: Helium
found: Formed by radioactive decay deep underground and trapped in natural-gas fields; also the second most abundant element in the universe.
uses: Cooling the superconducting magnets in MRI scanners, lifting balloons and airships, and creating inert atmospheres for welding.
daily: The gas that makes party balloons float and that keeps hospital MRI machines cold enough to work.

name: Lithium
found: In brine pools and pegmatite rocks; major deposits lie in the salt flats of Chile, Argentina and Bolivia, and in Australian spodumene mines.
uses: Rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, heat-resistant glass and ceramics, and as a mood-stabilising medicine.
daily: The battery in your phone, laptop and electric car relies on lithium to store and release charge.

name: Beryllium
found: In the minerals beryl and bertrandite; gemstone forms include emerald and aquamarine.
uses: Lightweight, stiff alloys for aerospace, X-ray windows, and precision instruments because it is transparent to X-rays.
daily: Found in the mirrors of space telescopes and in the springs and contacts of some electronics.

name: Boron
found: In borax and other borate minerals, concentrated in dry lake beds such as those in Turkey and California.
uses: Heat-resistant borosilicate glass, detergents, fertilisers, and neutron-absorbing control rods in nuclear reactors.
daily: Borax in laundry boosters and the tough Pyrex-type glass of your oven dishes both depend on boron.

name: Carbon
found: In all living things, in coal, oil and natural gas, and as graphite and diamond; carbon dioxide cycles through the air and oceans.
uses: Steelmaking, plastics, fuels, carbon-fibre composites, and the graphite in pencils and electrodes.
daily: Every living cell in your body is built on carbon, and it is the 'lead' in your pencil and the diamond in a ring.

name: Nitrogen
found: Makes up about 78% of the air you breathe; also bound into proteins, DNA and soil nitrates.
uses: Making ammonia and fertilisers, freezing and preserving food, and providing an inert blanket in packaging and chemistry.
daily: Most of every breath you take is nitrogen, and it keeps bagged snacks fresh by filling the empty space.

name: Oxygen
found: About 21% of the atmosphere, the larger part of water by mass, and nearly half the Earth's crust.
uses: Breathing support in medicine, steelmaking, water treatment, and rocket oxidiser.
daily: The gas you cannot live without — every cell uses it to release energy from food.

name: Fluorine
found: In the minerals fluorite and fluorapatite; too reactive to exist free in nature.
uses: Non-stick coatings (PTFE), refrigerants, etching glass, and uranium processing.
daily: Fluoride in toothpaste and tap water that hardens tooth enamel and fights decay.

name: Neon
found: A trace gas in the atmosphere, separated by cooling and distilling liquid air.
uses: Glowing advertising signs, high-voltage indicators, and some lasers.
daily: The classic orange-red glow of a 'neon' sign in a shop window.

name: Sodium
found: Never free in nature — locked into rock salt, seawater and many minerals.
uses: Table salt and baking soda (as compounds), street-lamp vapour, and a coolant in some reactors.
daily: Half of the salt on your chips; your nerves also fire using sodium ions.

name: Magnesium
found: In seawater and the minerals dolomite and magnesite; the eighth most abundant element in the crust.
uses: Lightweight alloys for cars and laptops, fireworks and flares, and antacids.
daily: The bright white flame of a sparkler, and the magnesium in leafy greens your body needs.

name: Aluminium
found: The most abundant metal in the crust, mined as bauxite ore.
uses: Drink cans, foil, aircraft and car bodies, window frames and power lines.
daily: The can your soft drink comes in and the foil you wrap leftovers in.

name: Silicon
found: In sand and quartz; the second most abundant element in the Earth's crust.
uses: Computer chips and solar cells, glass, and silicone rubbers and sealants.
daily: The chip inside your phone and computer, and the glass in your windows, both start as silicon.

name: Phosphorus
found: In phosphate rock and in every living cell's DNA, bones and teeth.
uses: Fertilisers, matches, detergents, and food additives.
daily: It strikes your matches alight and builds the calcium phosphate in your bones and teeth.

name: Sulfur
found: Near volcanoes and hot springs as bright yellow deposits, and in many ores and crude oil.
uses: Making sulfuric acid, vulcanising rubber, fertilisers, and fungicides.
daily: The yellow powder that toughens rubber tyres and the smell of a struck match.

name: Chlorine
found: As chloride in seawater and rock salt; too reactive to exist free.
uses: Disinfecting drinking water and pools, bleaching, and making PVC plastic.
daily: The chemical that keeps swimming pools and tap water safe to use.

name: Argon
found: Almost 1% of the atmosphere, separated from liquefied air.
uses: Filling light bulbs and double-glazed windows, and shielding welds.
daily: The inert gas inside many light bulbs that stops the filament burning out.

name: Potassium
found: In potash deposits and many minerals; an essential nutrient in soil and food.
uses: Potassium fertilisers, soaps, and salt substitutes.
daily: The mineral in bananas and potatoes that helps your heart and muscles work.

name: Calcium
found: In limestone, chalk, marble and gypsum, and in seashells and bones.
uses: Cement and concrete, plaster, steelmaking, and dietary supplements.
daily: The calcium that builds your bones and teeth, and the limestone in cement and chalk.

name: Scandium
found: Thinly spread in many minerals; commercially recovered as a by-product.
uses: Strong, light aluminium-scandium alloys for aerospace and high-end bike frames, and bright stadium lamps.
daily: The intense white light of some sports-stadium floodlights comes from scandium lamps.

name: Titanium
found: In the minerals rutile and ilmenite; the ninth most abundant element in the crust.
uses: Strong, light, corrosion-proof parts for aircraft and implants, and titanium-dioxide white pigment.
daily: The white in paint, sunscreen and toothpaste, and the metal in hip and knee implants.

name: Vanadium
found: In about 65 different minerals and in some crude oils.
uses: Strengthening steel for tools and springs, and in large grid-storage flow batteries.
daily: The tough steel in spanners and high-strength car parts is often vanadium steel.

name: Chromium
found: Mined as chromite ore, mainly in South Africa and Kazakhstan.
uses: Stainless steel, shiny chrome plating, and green and other pigments.
daily: The mirror-bright chrome on taps and bike parts, and the metal that makes cutlery stainless.

name: Manganese
found: In many ores and in deep-sea nodules; an essential trace nutrient.
uses: Toughening steel, making dry-cell and lithium batteries, and purple-pink glass.
daily: It hardens the steel in railway tracks and is the cathode in many torch batteries.

name: Iron
found: The Earth's core is mostly iron; mined from ore such as haematite.
uses: Steel for buildings, vehicles, tools and machinery — the backbone of industry.
daily: The steel in buildings, cars and cutlery, and the iron in your blood that carries oxygen.

name: Cobalt
found: In ores alongside nickel and copper, much of it from the Democratic Republic of Congo.
uses: Rechargeable battery cathodes, hard cutting tools, magnets, and deep-blue pigments.
daily: A key ingredient in phone and electric-car batteries, and the rich blue of some pottery glazes.

name: Nickel
found: In sulfide and laterite ores, and in iron-nickel meteorites.
uses: Stainless steel, rechargeable batteries, coins, and corrosion-resistant plating.
daily: Mixed into stainless-steel sinks and cutlery and used to plate many shiny metal parts.

name: Copper
found: As native metal and in ores such as chalcopyrite; large mines in Chile.
uses: Electrical wiring, plumbing, motors, and alloys like brass and bronze.
daily: The wiring that carries electricity through your home and the pipes that bring water.

name: Zinc
found: In the ore sphalerite; an essential trace nutrient for life.
uses: Galvanising steel against rust, making brass, batteries, and sunscreen.
daily: The coating that stops garden gates and roofs rusting, and the zinc in cold lozenges.

name: Gallium
found: A by-product of aluminium and zinc refining; no ore of its own.
uses: LED lights, fast computer chips, solar cells, and low-melting alloys.
daily: The bright LEDs in your screens, torches and traffic lights rely on gallium compounds.

name: Germanium
found: In zinc ores and some coals; recovered during smelting.
uses: Fibre-optic cables, infrared night-vision lenses, and electronics.
daily: The glass fibres that carry your internet and the lenses in thermal-imaging cameras.

name: Arsenic
found: In sulfide minerals such as arsenopyrite, often with gold and copper.
uses: Semiconductors (gallium arsenide), wood preservatives, and some alloys; notoriously toxic.
daily: Mostly an industrial and historical poison; today found in some high-speed and solar electronics.

name: Selenium
found: In sulfide ores as a by-product of copper refining; a trace nutrient.
uses: Photocopier drums and solar cells, red glass, and anti-dandruff shampoos.
daily: The selenium in some shampoos and the trace amount in nuts your body needs.

name: Bromine
found: As bromide salts in seawater and salt-lake brines such as the Dead Sea.
uses: Flame retardants, water treatment, and some dyes and medicines.
daily: Flame-retardant coatings in electronics and furniture once relied heavily on bromine.

name: Krypton
found: A trace gas in the atmosphere, separated from liquid air.
uses: Energy-saving windows, high-performance lighting, and some lasers.
daily: Krypton fills some double-glazed windows to improve their insulation.

name: Rubidium
found: In trace amounts in minerals like lepidolite; recovered as a by-product.
uses: Atomic clocks, specialty glass, and research electronics.
daily: Rubidium atomic clocks help keep GPS and phone networks precisely on time.

name: Strontium
found: In the minerals celestine and strontianite.
uses: Bright red fireworks and flares, ceramic magnets, and glow-in-the-dark paints.
daily: The vivid red bursts in fireworks displays come from burning strontium salts.

name: Yttrium
found: In rare-earth ores such as monazite and xenotime.
uses: Red phosphors in older screens, LED and laser materials, and strong ceramics.
daily: Yttrium phosphors produced the red colour in older colour TVs and help make white LEDs.

name: Zirconium
found: In the mineral zircon, often in beach sands.
uses: Nuclear-reactor cladding, heat-resistant ceramics, and gemstone imitations (cubic zirconia).
daily: Cubic zirconia 'diamonds' in jewellery and the tough ceramic in some knife blades.

name: Niobium
found: In the minerals columbite and pyrochlore, mostly mined in Brazil.
uses: Strengthening steel for pipelines and cars, and superconducting magnets.
daily: A pinch of niobium makes the high-strength steel in gas pipelines and car frames.

name: Molybdenum
found: In the ore molybdenite; an essential trace nutrient.
uses: High-strength, heat-resistant steel alloys, lubricants, and catalysts.
daily: Molybdenum steel makes engine parts and tools that stay strong when hot.

name: Technetium
found: The lightest element with no stable form — essentially absent from nature and made artificially.
uses: Its short-lived isotope is the workhorse tracer of medical imaging.
daily: Technetium-99m is injected for many hospital scans of the heart, bones and organs.

name: Ruthenium
found: With platinum metals in ores from South Africa and Russia.
uses: Hard-wearing electrical contacts, hard-disk coatings, and catalysts.
daily: Ruthenium thin films help pack more data onto computer hard drives.

name: Rhodium
found: A rare by-product of platinum and nickel mining.
uses: The most active metal in catalytic converters, and bright reflective plating.
daily: Rhodium in your car's catalytic converter cleans up exhaust gases.

name: Palladium
found: With platinum metals; major sources are Russia and South Africa.
uses: Catalytic converters, electronics, dentistry, and jewellery (white gold).
daily: Palladium scrubs pollutants from petrol-car exhausts and appears in white-gold rings.

name: Silver
found: As native silver and in ores with lead, copper and gold.
uses: Jewellery and cutlery, electrical contacts, solar cells, and antibacterial coatings.
daily: The metal in fine jewellery and cutlery, and the best electrical conductor known.

name: Cadmium
found: A by-product of zinc refining.
uses: Rechargeable NiCd batteries, pigments, and corrosion-resistant plating; toxic.
daily: Older rechargeable 'NiCd' batteries and bright yellow artists' pigments used cadmium.

name: Indium
found: A trace by-product of zinc mining.
uses: The transparent conductive coating on touchscreens (indium tin oxide), and solders.
daily: The invisible conductive layer that lets your phone and tablet screens sense your touch.

name: Tin
found: In the ore cassiterite.
uses: Solder for electronics, tin-plating steel cans, and alloys like bronze and pewter.
daily: The solder holding electronics together and the tin lining inside food cans.

name: Antimony
found: In the ore stibnite, much of it mined in China.
uses: Flame retardants, lead-acid battery alloys, and some semiconductors.
daily: Antimony compounds make many plastics and fabrics resist catching fire.

name: Tellurium
found: A rare by-product of copper refining.
uses: Thin-film solar panels, alloying to make metals easier to machine, and some electronics.
daily: Tellurium is a key ingredient in some of the world's large solar-power farms.

name: Iodine
found: As iodide in seawater, seaweed and natural brines.
uses: Antiseptics, adding iodine to table salt, and X-ray contrast agents.
daily: The iodine added to table salt that keeps your thyroid gland healthy, and antiseptic on cuts.

name: Xenon
found: A very rare trace gas in the atmosphere.
uses: Bright car headlamps and camera flashes, anaesthesia, and ion thrusters for spacecraft.
daily: The brilliant white xenon headlights on some cars and the flash in professional cameras.

name: Caesium
found: In the mineral pollucite; recovered as a by-product of lithium mining.
uses: The most accurate atomic clocks, oil-drilling fluids, and some electronics.
daily: The caesium atomic clock is the official definition of the second, keeping the world's time.

name: Barium
found: In the minerals barite and witherite.
uses: The 'barium meal' for X-rays, drilling muds, and green fireworks.
daily: The barium drink that makes your stomach show up clearly on a medical X-ray.

name: Lanthanum
found: In rare-earth ores such as monazite and bastnäsite.
uses: Camera and telescope lenses, hybrid-car batteries, and catalysts.
daily: Lanthanum makes the high-quality glass in camera lenses and the batteries in hybrid cars.

name: Cerium
found: The most abundant rare-earth element, in monazite and bastnäsite.
uses: Polishing glass, catalytic converters, and the 'flint' in lighters.
daily: The spark that lights your gas lighter comes from a cerium alloy striker.

name: Praseodymium
found: In rare-earth ores alongside neodymium.
uses: Powerful magnets, green-tinted welding goggles, and aircraft engine alloys.
daily: Praseodymium tints welders' goggles to protect their eyes from glare.

name: Neodymium
found: In monazite and bastnäsite rare-earth ores.
uses: The strongest permanent magnets known, plus lasers and glass colouring.
daily: Tiny neodymium magnets power the speakers in your earbuds and the motors in cordless tools.

name: Promethium
found: Essentially absent from nature; produced in nuclear reactors.
uses: Luminous paint and tiny atomic 'betavoltaic' batteries for research.
daily: Promethium once powered self-luminous dials and is too radioactive for everyday products today.

name: Samarium
found: In monazite and bastnäsite.
uses: Heat-stable samarium-cobalt magnets, and cancer-treatment isotopes.
daily: Samarium magnets keep working at high temperatures in headphones and precision motors.

name: Europium
found: In small amounts in rare-earth ores.
uses: Red and blue phosphors in screens and energy-saving lamps, and anti-counterfeit marks.
daily: Europium glows under UV light in the security marks printed on banknotes.

name: Gadolinium
found: In monazite and bastnäsite.
uses: MRI contrast agents, neutron shielding, and magnetic-cooling research.
daily: A gadolinium injection sharpens the detail of many MRI scans.

name: Terbium
found: In rare-earth ores, in tiny amounts.
uses: Green phosphors in displays and lamps, and powerful magnetostrictive alloys.
daily: Terbium produces the green colour in many TV screens and fluorescent lights.

name: Dysprosium
found: In rare-earth ores such as xenotime.
uses: Heat-resistant magnets for wind turbines and electric cars, and laser materials.
daily: Dysprosium keeps electric-car and wind-turbine magnets working when they get hot.

name: Holmium
found: In monazite, in trace amounts.
uses: Surgical and dental lasers, and the strongest magnetic fields in research magnets.
daily: Holmium lasers are used by surgeons to break up kidney stones.

name: Erbium
found: In rare-earth ores.
uses: Amplifiers in fibre-optic cables, pink glass and glazes, and lasers.
daily: Erbium amplifiers boost the light signals carrying your internet across oceans.

name: Thulium
found: The rarest stable rare-earth, in trace amounts in ores.
uses: Portable X-ray sources and high-efficiency lasers.
daily: Thulium powers compact, battery-run X-ray machines used in the field.

name: Ytterbium
found: In monazite and other rare-earth ores.
uses: The most precise optical atomic clocks, lasers, and stress gauges.
daily: Ytterbium optical clocks are so accurate they would not lose a second over billions of years.

name: Lutetium
found: The rarest and most expensive rare-earth, in trace amounts.
uses: PET-scan detectors, petroleum refining catalysts, and research.
daily: Lutetium crystals detect the radiation in hospital PET cancer scans.

name: Hafnium
found: Always alongside zirconium in the mineral zircon.
uses: Nuclear-reactor control rods, advanced computer chips, and superalloys.
daily: Hafnium in the insulating layer of modern microchips lets them run faster and cooler.

name: Tantalum
found: In the ores tantalite and coltan.
uses: Tiny high-capacity capacitors in electronics, and corrosion-proof surgical implants.
daily: Tantalum capacitors pack power into the small circuit boards of phones and laptops.

name: Tungsten
found: In the ores wolframite and scheelite.
uses: Light-bulb and furnace filaments, cutting tools, and heavy alloys.
daily: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal — the glowing filament in old bulbs and the tips of drill bits.

name: Rhenium
found: One of the rarest elements, recovered from molybdenum ores.
uses: Jet-engine and rocket alloys, and petroleum-refining catalysts.
daily: Rhenium superalloys let jet engines run hotter and more efficiently.

name: Osmium
found: With platinum metals; the densest naturally occurring element.
uses: Very hard alloys for pen tips, electrical contacts, and instrument pivots.
daily: Osmium alloys once tipped fountain pens and still make hard-wearing instrument bearings.

name: Iridium
found: With platinum metals; concentrated in some meteorite impact layers.
uses: Spark-plug tips, crucibles for growing crystals, and corrosion-proof contacts.
daily: Iridium-tipped spark plugs last far longer in car engines.

name: Platinum
found: As native metal and with nickel and copper ores; mostly from South Africa.
uses: Catalytic converters, jewellery, lab equipment, and cancer drugs.
daily: Platinum in catalytic converters cleans car exhaust, and it sets fine jewellery.

name: Gold
found: As native gold in veins and river gravels; known since antiquity.
uses: Jewellery, money and reserves, electronics contacts, and dentistry.
daily: The gold in rings and the micro-thin gold contacts in your phone's connectors.

name: Mercury
found: In the ore cinnabar; the only metal liquid at room temperature.
uses: Older thermometers and switches, fluorescent lamps, and gold extraction; toxic.
daily: The silvery liquid in old thermometers and the vapour that lights fluorescent tubes.

name: Thallium
found: In trace amounts in sulfide ores.
uses: Infrared detectors and, historically, rodent poison; highly toxic.
daily: Mostly an industrial hazard today; once used in rat poison and now in some infrared sensors.

name: Lead
found: In the ore galena; known and used since antiquity.
uses: Car batteries, radiation shielding, and weights; toxic, so banned from petrol and paint.
daily: The lead-acid battery that starts your car, and the apron that shields you at the dentist.

name: Bismuth
found: In the minerals bismuthinite and bismite, and as native metal.
uses: Stomach medicines, low-melting alloys and solders, and cosmetics.
daily: The active ingredient in pink stomach-settling medicines like Pepto-Bismol.

name: Polonium
found: Extremely rare; forms in trace amounts in uranium ores.
uses: Anti-static devices and lightweight heat sources for spacecraft; intensely radioactive.
daily: No everyday use — polonium is dangerously radioactive and tightly controlled.

name: Astatine
found: The rarest naturally occurring element; only trace amounts exist at any moment.
uses: A candidate for targeted cancer radiotherapy in research.
daily: No everyday use — astatine is so rare and short-lived it exists only in tiny research quantities.

name: Radon
found: A radioactive gas from the decay of uranium in rocks and soil.
uses: Studied for cancer therapy; mainly a hazard to monitor in buildings.
daily: Radon can seep into basements from the ground, so homes in some areas are tested for it.

name: Francium
found: Vanishingly rare; forms briefly in uranium and thorium decay.
uses: Pure research into atomic structure only.
daily: No everyday use — francium's longest-lived form lasts only about 22 minutes.

name: Radium
found: In uranium ores; isolated by the Curies from pitchblende.
uses: Once in luminous paint and early cancer therapy; now largely replaced.
daily: Historically painted on glow-in-the-dark watch dials, now avoided because it is dangerously radioactive.

name: Actinium
found: In trace amounts in uranium ores.
uses: A neutron source and a candidate for targeted cancer therapy.
daily: No everyday use — actinium is intensely radioactive and confined to research.

name: Thorium
found: More abundant than uranium; in the mineral monazite.
uses: A potential nuclear fuel, gas-lantern mantles (historically), and alloys.
daily: Thorium once made camping-lantern mantles glow brightly and is studied as a future reactor fuel.

name: Protactinium
found: In trace amounts in uranium ores.
uses: Scientific research only; rare and radioactive.
daily: No everyday use — protactinium is scarce, costly and highly radioactive.

name: Uranium
found: In the ores uraninite (pitchblende) and others worldwide.
uses: Fuel for nuclear power stations and naval reactors, and (historically) weapons.
daily: Uranium fuels nuclear power plants that supply electricity to millions of homes.

name: Neptunium
found: Only trace natural amounts; mostly made in reactors.
uses: A precursor for making plutonium-238 and in neutron-detection research.
daily: No everyday use — neptunium is a by-product of nuclear reactors used in research.

name: Plutonium
found: Essentially man-made in reactors; only traces occur naturally.
uses: Nuclear reactor fuel, weapons, and long-lived power sources for deep-space probes.
daily: Plutonium-238 has powered NASA probes like Voyager and the Mars rovers for decades.

name: Americium
found: Man-made in nuclear reactors.
uses: The ionising source in household smoke detectors, and industrial gauges.
daily: A tiny, safely sealed speck of americium makes your home smoke alarm work.

name: Curium
found: Man-made in reactors and accelerators.
uses: Compact power and heat sources, and X-ray spectrometers on space probes.
daily: Curium-powered instruments analysed the soil on Mars rovers; no household use.

name: Berkelium
found: Man-made in tiny amounts in reactors and accelerators.
uses: Making heavier elements in the laboratory.
daily: No everyday use — berkelium is produced in microgram amounts for research.

name: Californium
found: Man-made; a few grams are produced worldwide each year.
uses: A portable neutron source for oil-well surveying, medicine and detecting metals.
daily: Californium neutron sources help scan for gold and oil deep underground.

name: Einsteinium
found: Man-made; first found in the debris of a 1952 hydrogen-bomb test.
uses: Pure research, including making heavier elements.
daily: No everyday use — einsteinium exists only in research-scale amounts.

name: Fermium
found: Man-made; also first identified in 1952 bomb-test debris.
uses: Scientific research only.
daily: No everyday use — fermium cannot be produced in weighable amounts.

name: Mendelevium
found: Man-made one atom at a time in accelerators.
uses: Pure research into the heaviest elements.
daily: No everyday use — mendelevium is made only a few atoms at a time.

name: Nobelium
found: Man-made in accelerators.
uses: Pure research only.
daily: No everyday use — nobelium exists only fleetingly in laboratories.

name: Lawrencium
found: Man-made in accelerators.
uses: Pure research only.
daily: No everyday use — lawrencium is made an atom at a time for study.

name: Rutherfordium
found: Man-made by colliding nuclei in accelerators.
uses: Research into the chemistry of superheavy elements.
daily: No everyday use — rutherfordium atoms last only seconds.

name: Dubnium
found: Man-made in accelerators.
uses: Pure research only.
daily: No everyday use — dubnium exists only in single-atom amounts.

name: Seaborgium
found: Man-made in accelerators.
uses: Pure research only.
daily: No everyday use — seaborgium is studied one atom at a time.

name: Bohrium
found: Man-made in accelerators.
uses: Pure research only.
daily: No everyday use — bohrium atoms decay within seconds.

name: Hassium
found: Man-made in accelerators.
uses: Pure research only.
daily: No everyday use — hassium is made in vanishingly small amounts.

name: Meitnerium
found: Man-made in accelerators.
uses: Pure research only.
daily: No everyday use — meitnerium exists only as a handful of atoms.

name: Darmstadtium
found: Man-made in accelerators.
uses: Pure research only.
daily: No everyday use — darmstadtium decays almost instantly.

name: Roentgenium
found: Man-made in accelerators.
uses: Pure research only.
daily: No everyday use — roentgenium is among the rarest substances ever made.

name: Copernicium
found: Man-made in accelerators.
uses: Pure research only.
daily: No everyday use — copernicium exists only fleetingly in laboratories.

name: Nihonium
found: Man-made; first confirmed at RIKEN in Japan.
uses: Pure research only.
daily: No everyday use — nihonium atoms last a fraction of a second.

name: Flerovium
found: Man-made in accelerators.
uses: Pure research only.
daily: No everyday use — flerovium is made one atom at a time.

name: Moscovium
found: Man-made in accelerators.
uses: Pure research only.
daily: No everyday use — moscovium exists only in research.

name: Livermorium
found: Man-made in accelerators.
uses: Pure research only.
daily: No everyday use — livermorium decays in milliseconds.

name: Tennessine
found: Man-made; one of the most recently created elements.
uses: Pure research only.
daily: No everyday use — tennessine has only ever been made as a few atoms.

name: Oganesson
found: Man-made; the heaviest element yet created.
uses: Pure research only.
daily: No everyday use — oganesson is the heaviest known element and exists only fleetingly.
